scope: Authoritative NASA entry-profile reference quantities for bounded Artemis I versus Artemis II trajectory comparison

evidence_items.claim: NASA's Artemis I entry-performance reconstruction defines Entry Interface at 400,000 ft geodetic altitude and reports an actual inertial velocity magnitude of 36,062.65680 ft/s.
evidence_items.interpretation: Provides a technically matched Artemis I inertial Entry Interface speed for comparison with the Artemis II high-rate source-state inertial speed magnitude.
limitations: The Artemis I state is reported by NASA from flight reconstruction.
Frame conventions must remain explicit when comparing individual vector components.
Only velocity magnitude is used for the cross-mission speed comparison because magnitude is invariant under pure frame rotation.

evidence_items.claim: NASA reports that Artemis I successfully performed a skip entry and reached an actual skip-apogee geodetic altitude of 287.4 kft, compared with a predicted 293.5 kft.
evidence_items.interpretation: Defines the principal published Artemis I upper-trajectory skip landmark.
limitations: Skip-apogee altitude is not the same quantity as rebound amplitude.
The Artemis I skip apogee must not be interpreted as an Artemis II design requirement.
MissionLab does not currently reconstruct the full Artemis I state history from raw flight data.

evidence_items.claim: NASA's Artemis I entry-performance paper identifies first and second peak sensed-acceleration magnitudes of 4.05 g and 3.89 g.
evidence_items.interpretation: Provides qualitative heritage context for the two-pass Artemis I skip-entry loading structure.
limitations: These values are sensed acceleration magnitudes.
They are not directly comparable to Phase 2C MissionLab kinematic deceleration divided by g0.
MissionLab must not describe its Phase 2C g0-equivalent quantity as crew g-load.

evidence_items.claim: NASA's Artemis I mission timeline reports crew-module Entry Interface at MET 025/11:15:52 and splashdown at MET 025/11:36:27, a difference of 1,235 seconds.
evidence_items.interpretation: Provides an authoritative Artemis I Entry Interface to splashdown duration.
limitations: The Artemis II comparison endpoint is a MissionLab-derived WGS84 surface crossing correlated with NASA's splashdown minute.
The cross-mission duration comparison therefore mixes NASA-reported Artemis I event epochs with a derived Artemis II terminal epoch.

evidence_items.claim: NASA technical reporting states that Artemis II flew a modified trajectory without the Artemis I skip entry to minimize the crack-inducing conditions identified during the Artemis I heat-shield investigation.
evidence_items.source_title: Under Pressure: The Artemis I Heatshield Char Loss Investigation and Artemis II's Successful Entry
evidence_items.interpretation: Defines the authoritative terminology boundary for Artemis II.
limitations: A geometric altitude rebound in the Artemis II trajectory must not be relabeled as a skip entry.
The source does not publish the full Artemis II guidance design or trajectory optimization constraint set.

evidence_items.claim: NASA described the Artemis II Orion return sequence in public mission coverage as a lofted entry sequence.
evidence_items.source_title: Artemis II Flight Day 9: Crew Prepares to Come Home
evidence_items.interpretation: Supports describing MissionLab's derived Artemis II vertical rebound as a loft/rebound while preserving NASA's explicit no-skip classification.
limitations: The phrase is a NASA public mission label rather than a complete mathematical guidance-mode definition.

evidence_items.claim: NASA reported that Orion would reach approximately 23,864 mph maximum velocity just before Artemis II Entry Interface.
evidence_items.source_title: Artemis II Flight Day 9: Crew Prepares to Come Home
evidence_items.interpretation: Retained as public mission context rather than the primary cross-mission speed comparison.
limitations: This public velocity value is not used as the primary speed-comparison metric because its reporting semantics are not as precisely matched to the Artemis I technical EI inertial state.
MissionLab instead compares the technical Artemis I EI inertial velocity magnitude with the Artemis II high-rate source-state inertial speed magnitude.

primary_metrics.artemis_ii_quantity: NASA flight-derived high-rate M50 inertial speed magnitude

context_only_metrics: Artemis II public maximum velocity just before Entry Interface

planned_figures.purpose: Compare Artemis I NASA-reported EI-to-splashdown duration with Artemis II MissionLab-derived EI-to-surface-crossing duration.
Compare Artemis I NASA-reported skip apogee with Artemis II MissionLab-derived rebound-top altitude while preserving different trajectory classifications.
Show the actual Artemis II derived altitude rebound versus Entry Interface elapsed time with descent-to-climb and climb-to-descent markers.

interpretation_guardrails: Artemis II must not be labeled a skip entry.
The Artemis II derived vertical rebound may be described as a rebound or loft.
Artemis I skip-apogee altitude and Artemis II rebound-top altitude may be compared as upper-profile landmarks but not as identical guidance phases.
The Artemis I to Artemis II duration comparison must preserve mixed provenance between NASA-reported Artemis I epochs and the MissionLab-derived Artemis II surface crossing.
Public mission velocity figures are context only when epoch or frame semantics are not matched.
The primary speed comparison must use inertial velocity magnitudes with explicitly compatible semantics.
Artemis I sensed acceleration must not be directly compared with Phase 2C MissionLab g0-equivalent kinematic deceleration.
No trajectory comparison may be converted into a TPS char-loss or damage prediction.
No causal claim may be made that every Artemis I versus Artemis II entry-profile difference was driven exclusively by the heat-shield investigation.
